The BWA 2.0 is equipped with state-of-the-art 3MHz technology and provides extensive research parameters for professionals to better suit diverse patients with diff erent conditions and medical specialties than ever before. Through this, InBody provides more parameters which can be used in various clinical fi elds to pre-screen diseases and evaluate nutritional status. Direct Segmental Measurement-BIA Each of our body segments is diff erent in length and cross-sectional area. Arms and legs are longer and narrower in comparison to the trunk, so their impedance values are higher than the trunk. On the other hand, the trunk is shorter and wider than the arms and legs, so its impedance value is lower. However, the trunk muscle mass accounts for almost half of the whole body muscle mass, which is why a small impedance change in the trunk has a greater impact on the amount of whole body muscle mass. Therefore, the trunk must be measured separately in order to measure the whole body muscle mass accurately. To calculate the body composition by these conventional BIA devices, they needed to add statistical data such as age and gender in order to calculate results. However, InBody overcame these limitations with technologies of using Multi-Frequency, Direct Segmental Measurement, and 16-Point Clamp Electrodes System so that BWA provides results that are not aff ected by age, ethnicity or gender. Only reference ranges or scores based on age and gender are used as a basis for evaluating the values determined. Impedance is the resistance of the human body generated when a micro alternating current flows through the human body. The human body is made of water that conducts electricity well, and the resistance varies depending on the amount of water. BIA is a technology that quantitatively measures body water through impedance that occurs when an electric current flows through the human body. InBody provides diverse information on body composition based on the measured body water. InBody does not rely on empirical estimations based on age, gender, and more to ensure the accuracy of the measured data. In the past, empirical estimations were applied to the equations to ensure accuracy due to technological limitations. However, this resulted in lower accuracy when the measured population group changes. InBody overcame these limitations with technological developments such as direct segmental measurement-BIA to measure and analyze accurate body composition without applying empirical estimation.

PBF FFMI the New Era The Evolution of Health Indicator After using weight scale to measure human body, people started to think of weight and health together. BMI was the indicator of whether you are underweight, normal or overweigh by only using height and weight. Paradigm shift of your health indicator While simple and inexpensive, BMI often faced vigorous debate regarding health evaluation. Impedance is the resistance of the human body generated when a micro alternating current flows through the human body. The human body is made of water that conducts electricity well, and the resistance varies depending on the amount of water. BIA is a technology that quantitatively measures body water through impedance that occurs when an electric current flows through the human body. InBody provides diverse information on body composition based on the measured body water. InBody does not rely on empirical estimations based on age, gender, and more to ensure the accuracy of the measured data. In the past, empirical estimations were applied to the equations to ensure accuracy due to technological limitations. However, this resulted in lower accuracy when the measured population group changes. InBody overcame these limitations with technological developments such as direct segmental measurement-BIA to measure and analyze accurate body composition without applying empirical estimation.

InBody uses Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA) technology to measure human body composition. Impedance is the resistance of the human body generated when a micro alternating current flows through the human body. The human body is made of water that conducts electricity well, and the resistance varies depending on the amount of water. BIA is a technology that quantitatively measures body water through impedance that occurs when an electric current flows through the human body. InBody provides diverse information on body composition based on the measured body water. InBody introduced a technology in body composition analyzers to trant multiple frequencies at once, obtaining specific impedance data for each for the first time. This reduces measurement time and error, leading to more accurate body water and fluid balance measurements.

Simultaneous Multi-Frequency Impedance Measurement The human body exhibits varying lengths and cross-sectional areas for each body segments. Arms and legs, characterized by narrow cross-sectional areas and length, exhibit higher impedance values and lower muscle mass. Conversely, the trunk, with its broader cross- sectional area, yields lower impedance values and higher muscle mass. Even the slightest change in trunk impedance can significantly influence the total muscle mass. Therefore, it is essential to separately measure trunk impedance for precise total muscle mass assessment. InBody conducts separate measurements for arms, legs, and the trunk, ensuring the utmost accuracy in the analysis. nt-BIA Each of our body segments is different in length and cross-sectional area. Arms and legs are longer and narrower in comparison to the trunk, so their impedance values are higher than the trunk. On the other hand, the trunk is shorter and wider than the arms and legs, so its impedance value is lower. However, the trunk muscle mass accounts for almost half of the whole body muscle mass, which is why a small impedance change in the trunk has a greater impact on the amount of whole body muscle mass. Therefore, the trunk must be measured separately in order to measure the whole body muscle mass accurately. However, when evaluating dialysis adequacy, urea is typically used. ① urea reduction ratio: URR ② fractional urea clearance: Kt/V K represents dialysis efficiency (ml/min), t represents dialysis time (min), V represents urea distribution volume (usually around 60% of body weight). Factors determining dialysis efficiency 1. Dialyzer performance (mainly membrane area): Larger membrane area results in increased dialysis efficiency. 2 Duration of dialysis: Typically 3-4 hours, but longer durations lead to increased dialysis efficiency. 3. Blood flow rate: Higher blood flow rates result in increased dialysis efficiency (usually 150-250 ml/min in Japan, 350 ml/min in the United States). 4. Dialysate flow rate: Higher dialysate flow rates also increase dialysis efficiency (typically 500 ml/min). When an Error Message pops up During the BWA Measurement In case of dry skin 01 The BWA is designed to stop the measurement if the contact resistance is high to ensure the precision and accuracy of the measurement. Subjects with excessively dry skin have high contact resistance. Therefore, if the skin is not moisturized enough, high contact resistance may affect the result. In case of wrong attachment position 02 If the BWA logo on the clamp is attached in the wrong position or direction, the measurement may cease. Check the attachment position again. In case the electrodes are not fully attached to the skin 03 If the measurement ceases again after the above options, the electrodes might be unattached from the skin. Especially for the ankle, the bone structure is large and complicated, so at least the upper part of the electrode must be in touch with the skin. c: Decoding Sarcopenic Obesity in Type 2 Diabetes through Body Composition Analysis Here is where your presentation begins Sarcopenic Obesity Prevalence 01 Prevalence Meta-analysis (20 studies): Overall prevalence in T2D ≈ 27%. Higher in North America (~30%), variable by assessment method (e.g., BIA: 24%). Elderly diabetics (≥65 years): 13–14% prevalence with poorer function in men. Some studies show rates up to 40% in diabetic populations. Sarcopenic obesity affects 13–40% of people with diabetes, highlighting the need for screening. Community older adults (≥65 yrs): SO ≈ 5.4%–6.3%. National survey (45 yrs+): possible sarcopenia ≈ 41.9%; SO ≈ 8.7%. Adults with T2D: sarcopenia ≈ 60%; SO ≈ 40%. Another study - Reported prevalence: 15–44% in diabetics. Risk factors: inactivity, inflammation, poor glycemic control, mitochondrial dysfunction. Sarcopenia linked with higher mortality and reduced quality of life. The treatment focusses on dietary protein intake (1.2-1.6 g/kg/day), vitamin D supplements, resistance and aerobic exercise, weight management (careful calorie restriction to avoid muscle loss), and blood glucose control. Sarcopenia negatively impacts T2DM outcomes, including quality of life and mortality. Early detection and combined lifestyle and pharmacological therapies are critical for controlling sarcopenia in diabetes individuals.

Pathophysiology The Vicious Cycle 02 Sequence of events: Excess adipose tissue → inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6). Inflammation → muscle protein breakdown and suppressed synthesis. Muscle loss → insulin resistance and reduced glucose disposal. Insulin resistance → further fat accumulation and mitochondrial dysfunction. Cycle perpetuates with aging, hormonal decline, and inactivity. Physical inactivity and poor nutrition worsen anabolic resistance, amplifying muscle mass decline and fat accumulation, creating a vicious cycle of sarcopenic obesity Reduced muscle strength and endurance causing difficulty in daily activities, slow walking speed, balance issues, and increased risk of falls and fractures. Excess fat leads to obesity-related symptoms like joint pain, limited physical function, fatigue, and respiratory difficulties. Increased risk of metabolic complications such as type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance due to combined muscle loss and fat gain. Higher likelihood of cardiovascular diseases including hypertension, atherosclerosis, heart failure, and increased all-cause mortality.

c: Hydration Guidelines Before InBody BIA Testing Adequate and consistent hydration is important for Bioelectrical Impedance Analysis (BIA), as the measurement is influenced by the distribution of body water. For reliable and comparable InBody results, it is recommended to maintain normal hydration and avoid both dehydration and excessive fluid intake immediately before the test. Recommended guidelines: • Maintain your usual hydration pattern before the InBody test. • Avoid drinking a large quantity of water immediately before the measurement. • If water has been consumed shortly before the test, it is recommended to allow at least 20 minutes before taking the InBody measurement. • Avoid testing immediately after strenuous exercise, as exercise can temporarily alter fluid distribution. • For repeated measurements, try to maintain similar testing conditions, preferably at a similar time of day and under similar food, fluid and activity conditions. • When possible, testing in a fasted or standardized state can help improve consistency between measurements. These recommendations are intended to improve measurement standardization and comparability, particularly when InBody measurements are being used to monitor changes over time.

Understanding the InBody Test Q. What is an InBody test? A. An InBody test uses bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA) to estimate body composition, such as body fat, lean mass, and body water. The parameters available depend on the device. Q. How is an InBody test different from a normal weighing scale? A. A weighing scale measures body weight. An InBody test provides additional body composition information, helping show how weight is distributed between fat and lean components. Q. How does InBody measure body composition? A. The device passes a low-level electrical current through the body and measures impedance. The measurements are used to estimate body composition. Q. Does an InBody test measure body fat directly? A. No. Body fat is estimated using bioelectrical measurements and the device's calculation method. Q. Can InBody tell me whether I am healthy? A.

ion. Q. Does an InBody test measure body fat directly? A. No. Body fat is estimated using bioelectrical measurements and the device's calculation method. Q. Can InBody tell me whether I am healthy? A. An InBody report provides body composition information, but it cannot determine overall health on its own. Results should be considered alongside medical history, examination, and other relevant assessments. 2. Before the Test Q. Should I eat before an InBody test? A. For more consistent results, it is generally recommended to test before eating or to follow the preparation instructions provided by the testing centre. Food and fluid intake can affect body weight and measurements. Q. Can I exercise before the test? A. Exercise may temporarily affect body water distribution and measurements. If possible, avoid testing immediately after exercise and follow the centre's preparation instructions. Q. Should I use the washroom before the test? A. Yes, when possible. Emptying the bladder before testing can help improve consistency between measurements. Q. Should I take the test at the same time of day? A. For comparisons over time, try to test at a similar time of day and under similar conditions. Q. Why do I need to remove shoes and socks? A. The device requires appropriate contact between the hands or feet and its electrodes. Follow the instructions for the specific device. Q.

Skeletal Muscle Mass estimates the amount of skeletal muscle in the body. It can help monitor changes in muscle mass over time. Q. What is Percent Body Fat (PBF)? A. Percent Body Fat is the percentage of total body weight attributed to fat mass. Q. What is Body Fat Mass? A. Body Fat Mass is the estimated total mass of fat in the body. Q. What is Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI)? A. SMI is an index used to assess skeletal muscle relative to body size. The calculation and clinical cut-offs depend on the method and guideline being used. Q. What is Visceral Fat Area (VFA)? A. Visceral Fat Area estimates the area of fat around the internal abdominal organs.

Visceral Fat Area estimates the area of fat around the internal abdominal organs. It should be interpreted according to the report guidance and clinical context. Q. What does ECW/TBW mean? A. ECW/TBW is the ratio of extracellular water to total body water. It provides information about body water distribution but is not, by itself, a diagnosis of fluid overload. Q. What is Phase Angle? A. Phase Angle is calculated from electrical resistance and reactance measurements. It is associated with cellular and tissue characteristics and should be interpreted in context. Q. What is segmental analysis? A. Segmental analysis shows estimated body composition in different body regions, such as the arms, legs, and trunk. Q. What does muscle imbalance mean on the report? A. It refers to a difference in estimated lean mass between body segments. Review the values and reference ranges shown on the specific report; the finding alone does not diagnose a condition. Q. Why can BMI be normal when body fat is high? A. BMI compares weight with height and does not distinguish fat mass from muscle mass. Body composition measurements provide additional information. 4. A. Results can vary with hydration, meals, exercise, time of day, recent bathroom use, posture, and electrode contact. Compare tests taken under similar conditions. Q. Can body fat or muscle mass change in a short time? A. True body composition changes usually take time, but estimates can fluctuate because of changes in body water and testing conditions. Q. How often should I repeat an InBody test? A. The interval depends on the reason for testing and the individual's care plan. Follow the recommendation of the healthcare professional or testing centre. Q. How can I compare two reports correctly? A. Compare reports taken under similar conditions and review trends across relevant parameters rather than relying on a single change. Q. Yes, body fat percentage may change when body weight or fat mass changes. Body Fat Percentage (%) = (Body Fat Mass ÷ Total Body Weight) × 100 For example, if body fat mass is 20 kg and total body weight is 80 kg, body fat percentage is 25%. If body weight changes, body fat percentage may increase or decrease depending on how fat mass and total body weight change relative to each other. It is also known as pinch test. As the name implies, this method involves pinching the subcutaneous fat layer with fingers and measuring the thickness using a caliper. Using the principle that approximately 50% of all body fat is stored as subcutaneous fat, the subcutaneous fat layer of triceps, abdominal, thigh, etc. is pinched at the epidermal layer and the thickness is measured using a caliper, readings of which is substituted into a set formula for calculation of body fat.

The subcutaneous fat layer thickness is substituted to the Jackson-Pollock formula for calculating body density and substituted to the Siri or Brozek formula for calculating Percent Body Fat. 1) Percent Body Fat by Brozek formula (%) = (457 - body density) - 414 2) Percent Body Fat by Siri formula (%) = (4.95 / body density - 4.50) x100 Advantages are the calipers easily portable, and measurement is simple and inexpensive. Although a large portion of body fat is found as subcutaneous fat, the measurement may not be accurate for people whose body fat distributions vary. With the patient lying down, photons of the X-ray beams of different energy levels scan the patient. It takes about 5 to 30 minutes. When the x-ray photons collide with an object, one of two things happen: photons get reflected or energy gets absorbed. Therefore, as the photons travel through an object, their energy level drops drastically. The loss of energy after passing through an object is proportional to the per-area weight of the object. Therefore, if the energy level of the x-ray is known and the attenuation coefficient of the object is known, the per-area weight of the object can be calculated. However, since the human body is not made of a single substance but consists of the BMC, lean, and fat as illustrated in Figure 2, dual energy x-ray is used. The ratio of the lower attenuation coefficient and the higher attenuation coefficient resulting from the two x-rays of different energy levels is called R-value, which is in linear correlation with Percent Body Fat for soft tissues. Therefore, the per pixel R-value by penetrating two X-ray beams through the body can provide the lean and fat ratios of a given tissue. When applying an external magnetic field the protons will align along the magnetic field. Since atomic nuclei can behave like magnets, the external magnetic field aligns the nuclei, which are then activated by a radio frequency wave. Once the radio wave is turned off, the activated nuclei will emit the signal absorbed; the emitted signal is used to develop the images through the use of a computer. This longitudinal magnetization of body tissues allows for the an external computer source to create images of the section of the body being examined based on the intrinsic properties of different tissue forms. This leads to impedance decrease in the bent area that results in decrease of PBF. 1. High Visceral Fat and Low SMI: Understanding Sarcopenic Obesity What does it mean? Sarcopenic obesity is the coexistence of excess adiposity and low muscle mass or muscle function. The ESPEN/EASO consensus recommends assessing excess body fat alongside muscle function and body composition when evaluating this condition (Donini et al., 2022). How to interpret the InBody findings InBody finding Interpretation Visceral Fat Level ≥10 or Visceral Fat Area ≥100 cm² Indicates elevated visceral adiposity relative to the applicable InBody reference values. Low Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI) May indicate low muscle mass when assessed using an appropriate calculation method and validated reference cut-off. Both findings together Suggests a body-composition pattern that warrants further evaluation for sarcopenic obesity. Clinical assessment: Muscle strength can be assessed using handgrip strength or other validated functional tests. The EWGSOP2 consensus identifies low muscle strength as the primary characteristic of sarcopenia, with low muscle quantity or quality used to confirm the diagnosis (Cruz-Jentoft et al., 2019). Understanding Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI) For this document, SMI is calculated using appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM), which represents the combined muscle mass of the arms and legs.

Understanding Skeletal Muscle Index (SMI) For this document, SMI is calculated using appendicular skeletal muscle mass (ASM), which represents the combined muscle mass of the arms and legs. Formula: SMI (kg/m²) = ASM (kg) ÷ Height² (m²) The Asian Working Group for Sarcopenia (AWGS 2019) recommends the following BIA-based cut-offs for low appendicular skeletal muscle mass index in Asian adults: Sex Low SMI Men Less than 7.0 kg/m² Women Less than 5.7 kg/m² Application to InBody data: Segmental Lean Analysis provides lean-mass values for the arms and legs. However, the sum of these segmental lean values should not automatically be assumed to represent validated ASM for clinical classification. A published 2025 letter has highlighted discrepancies between segmental lean totals and the reported skeletal muscle mass on InBody reports. For research purposes, the muscle-mass variable, calculation method and reference cut-offs should therefore be specified and validated before classifying participants as having low SMI. This is particularly important when analysing pre-operative and post-operative bariatric patients. 2. Understanding Segmental Lean and Segmental Fat Analysis Segmental Lean Analysis Segmental Lean Analysis provides information about lean mass across five body segments: right arm, left arm, trunk, right leg and left leg.

ntal Lean and Segmental Fat Analysis Segmental Lean Analysis Segmental Lean Analysis provides information about lean mass across five body segments: right arm, left arm, trunk, right leg and left leg. Parameter What it indicates Mass (kg) Lean mass measured for the respective body segment. Percentage (%) Comparison of the segment's lean mass with the device's reference value. Under, Normal or Over Indicates how the measured value compares with the applicable reference range. On applicable InBody models, approximately 90–110% represents the reference range for segmental lean mass. The exact range should be confirmed using the interpretation guide for the specific model. Segmental Fat Analysis Segmental Fat Analysis displays fat mass for the five body segments. Parameter What it indicates Fat Mass (kg) Estimated fat mass in the respective body segment. Percentage (%) Comparison with the device's reference value for segmental fat mass. Under, Normal or Over Indicates the measured value relative to the applicable reference range. On applicable InBody models, approximately 80–160% represents the reference range for segmental fat mass. BIA estimates body composition through electrical impedance and model-specific equations.

BIA estimates body composition through electrical impedance and model-specific equations. Hydration and fluid distribution can influence estimates; therefore, consistent measurement conditions are important when comparing results over time (Kyle et al., 2004). Understanding Left–Right Imbalance The displayed imbalance percentage represents the difference between the left and right segmental percentages, rather than the difference in mass in kilograms. Segment Balanced Slight imbalance Severe imbalance Arms Below 6% 6–10% Above 10% Legs Below 3% 3–5% Above 5% 3. Understanding the Percentages in Muscle-Fat Analysis Muscle-Fat Analysis displays three parameters: Weight, Skeletal Muscle Mass (SMM) and Body Fat Mass (BFM). The percentages compare measured values with the device's standard values based on the entered height and sex. Parameter Reference range Interpretation Weight Approximately 85–115% Compares measured weight with standard weight. Skeletal Muscle Mass Approximately 90–110% Compares measured SMM with standard SMM. Body Fat Mass Approximately 80–160% Compares measured fat mass with standard fat mass. These are general reference ranges for applicable report formats and should be checked against the relevant model's guide.

Mass Approximately 80–160% Compares measured fat mass with standard fat mass. These are general reference ranges for applicable report formats and should be checked against the relevant model's guide. These percentages indicate the measured value relative to the device's reference or standard value. They are not population percentiles and do not indicate an individual's rank within a population. Understanding D-, I- and C-shaped Patterns Pattern General appearance Interpretation D- shape The muscle bar is relatively longer than the weight and fat bars. Relatively higher muscle mass compared with the device's reference values. I-shape The three bars appear relatively similar. A comparatively balanced pattern across the displayed parameters. C- shape The weight and fat bars are relatively longer than the muscle bar. May indicate relatively higher fat mass with lower muscle mass compared with the reference values. These shapes are visual interpretation aids, not independent clinical diagnostic categories. The actual measurements and relevant clinical criteria should guide interpretation. A C-shaped pattern accompanied by elevated visceral fat and low SMI may warrant further evaluation for sarcopenic obesity, consistent with the ESPEN/EASO recommendation to assess adiposity, muscle mass and muscle function together (Donini et al., 2022). 4.

Understanding Target Weight, Fat Control and Muscle Control How is standard weight calculated? For the applicable InBody report format, the following values illustrate a reference approach to standard weight and body composition. Parameter Male Female Reference BMI 22 kg/m² 21.5 kg/m² Standard weight 22 × height² (m²) 21.5 × height² (m²) What do Fat Control and Muscle Control indicate? • Fat Control: Indicates the suggested change in fat mass towards the device's target body composition. • Muscle Control: Indicates the suggested change in muscle mass towards the device's target body composition. These values support body-composition assessment beyond body weight alone. The exact internal algorithm used to generate these recommendations is not established by the research references below; the values should therefore be interpreted according to the applicable device guidance. Impedance is the resistance that conducts electricity well, and the resistance varies depending on the amount of water. BIA is a technology that quantitatively information on body composition based on the measured body water. InBody does not rely on empirical estimations based on age, gender, and more to ensure the accuracy of the measured data. In the past, empirical estimations were applied to the equations to ensure accuracy due to technological limitations. However, this resulted in lower accuracy when the measured population group changes. InBody overcame these limitations with technological developments such as direct segmental measurement-BIA to measure and analyze accurate body composition without applying empirical estimation. Therefore, InBody devices can provide data No Estimations or Empirical Equations on Measured Values Using the structural features of the human body, InBody pioneered ‘8-Point Tactile electrode with Thumb Electrodes’. How to check Impedance measured by InBodyS10 Guide to evaluate measurement error Impedance value is the raw data directly measured from InBody. Impedance indicates resistance which disturbs the flow of alternating current. InBody measures this impedance by flowing a broad range of alternating current to the body through body water, and interpreting the body composition by interpreting these values. The measurement error can be detected by checking result sheet or LCD screen of InBodyS10. InBody sends alternating currents from low (1kHz) to high (1,000kHz) frequency to the body, and the high frequency flows through the cell membrane and flows along the whole body water. On the other hand, low frequency mainly flows along the extracellular water due to the resistance of the cell membrane which leads to the higher impedance than that of high frequency. Therefore, If the test is done in proper way, impedance is measured as above which reflects the characteristics of each frequency and body segment. In this background, the measurement error can be checked from the Impedance value in the right bottom of the result sheet or on a LCD result screen.

The visceral fat area is not directly measured by bioelectrical impedance measurement (BIA). However, the possibility of calculating visceral fat area through BIA method was suggested from the papers which studied the relationship between trunk impedance and visceral fat. 1),2) Based on this theoretical background, the visceral fat area provided by InBody is calculated from the regression formula of the visceral fat area taken by the CT scans. While doing this, BMI, fat free mass, body fat mass and percent body fat, and segmental lean muscle distribution are considered as well as the total body impedance obtained by the segmental measurement. In the case of the trunk, it consists of subcutaneous fat (intestinal fat), intestine lean (visceral muscle), visceral fat (visceral fat) accumulated in the subcutaneous tissue as shown below. Subcutaneous fat is present in the subcutaneous tissue and Rsub is connected in parallel to the current flowing vertically through the trunk. On the other hand, Intestine Lean and Visceral Fat can be seen to have a series of connection of Rin and Rvic for the current flowing vertically through the trunk.

On the other hand, Intestine Lean and Visceral Fat can be seen to have a series of connection of Rin and Rvic for the current flowing vertically through the trunk. Therefore, if Intestine Lean and Visceral Fat are unchanged and the subcutaneous fat increases, the outer wall of the fat thickens. However, electric current flows along the intestinal muscles, so the effect on the impedance is less. On the other hand, if there is no change in the subcutaneous fat and only Visceral Fat is increased, the series of connected Rvic increases and directly affects the impedance of the body, therefore it changes the size and the characteristics of the impedance. 1) Detection of segmental internal fat by bioelectrical impedance analysis in a biological phantom. SESSION 1 Basics of Body Composition Analysis Technology InBody India · Sales Training 04 Key Concept InBody is a Bioimpedance Analyzing device that measures Body Water, Skeletal Muscle Mass, Body Fat, Segmental Muscle Mass and more. Grabbing an electrical device with a wet hand is dangerous, since electricity flows through water well. Based on this theory, InBody uses Bio-Impedance Analysis: a small electrical current flows through the body, and the resistance (impedance) is measured to calculate body composition. KEY TAKEAWAY A small electrical current + the measured resistance (impedance) = body composition. What is BIA? SESSION 1 Basics of Body Composition Analysis Technology InBody India · Sales Training 05 Key Concept Relationship between Body Water and Impedance Electricity does not flow through FAT: the bulb stays OFF. Electricity flows through WATER: the bulb turns ON. KEY TAKEAWAY Resistance to electrical flow = Impedance. What is BIA?

Water and Impedance Electricity does not flow through FAT: the bulb stays OFF. Electricity flows through WATER: the bulb turns ON. KEY TAKEAWAY Resistance to electrical flow = Impedance. What is BIA? SESSION 1 Basics of Body Composition Analysis Technology InBody India · Sales Training 06 Key Concept Relationship between Body Water and Impedance High volume of water → current flows well → Low Impedance. Low volume of water → current does not flow well → High Impedance. KEY TAKEAWAY Impedance and body water are inversely proportional. BIA devices use impedance to measure body water. What is BIA? SESSION 1 Basics of Body Composition Analysis Technology InBody India · Sales Training 07 Key Concept The shape of the cylinder changes impedance Narrow and long cylinder = electricity does not flow well = High Impedance. Wide and short cylinder = electricity flows well = Low Impedance. KEY TAKEAWAY Same amount of water, but different impedance due to the shape of the cylinder. What is BIA? SESSION 1 Basics of Body Composition Analysis Technology InBody India · Sales Training 08 Key Concept How do we measure Body Water? The body is modelled as cylinders: arm, trunk and leg. Volume = Length × Area, and Impedance = ρ × Length / Area. Combining the two: Volume = ρ × Length² / Impedance. Using height as length, Total Body Water is proportional to Height² / Impedance, the Impedance Index.

Hysteresis, often caused by “elastic deformation,” occurs when a strain gauge dynamometer is used multiple times without allowing sufficient “cool down” time between measurements. c: Does the malnourished child with improper Body water content affect the 50khz trunk impedance value? Yes, a malnourished child with improper body water content significantly affects the 50kHz trunk impedance value. In bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA), impedance is the opposition to an electric current; because water and electrolytes are excellent conductors, changes in their volume and distribution directly alter this measurement. The trunk is a large, relatively short cylinder of the body. Even though it accounts for nearly 50% of total body weight, it contributes only a small fraction (about 10%) of total body impedance. Therefore, even minor changes in trunk fluid can cause noticeable shifts in the 50kHz impedance value. Fluid Overload (Oedematous Malnutrition/Kwashiorkor): Children with nutritional oedema have high levels of extracellular water (ECW) in the trunk. Because water conducts electricity easily, trunk impedance values will be significantly lower than normal. Dehydration (Severe Wasting/Marasmus): In children with marasmus or severe wasting who are also dehydrated, the loss of total body water (TBW) increases the resistance to current. In these cases, trunk impedance values will be significantly higher. Tissue Loss: Malnutrition involves the loss of muscle mass (the primary reservoir for intracellular water).

If yes, how can it still be considered for a malnourished child (MAM / SAM) as they have a poor hydration status and fat percentage? The 50 kHz frequency is the "gold standard" for Single-Frequency BIA (SFBIA) because it represents a point where the electrical current can partially penetrate cell membranes. The Cole Model: As discussed in the paper you linked (PMC10140124), 50 kHz is often very close to the Characteristic Frequency ($f_c$) in humans. At this frequency, the Reactance ($X_c$) is near its maximum, allowing for the best possible calculation of the Phase Angle (PhA). Validation Studies: Most predictive equations for Lean Body Mass (LBM) were developed and validated at 50 kHz because it provides a reliable balance between measuring extracellular fluid and reflecting cellular mass.

c: ration 3) As per our observation, the data that was valid had a phase angle value of zero. How can that be justifiable? A phase angle of zero at 50 kHz is physiologically unlikely in a living subject. Phase angle is calculated from: Reactance (Xc) Resistance (R) If phase angle is zero, it means: Reactance = 0 or Reactance was not recorded In the case of devices like the InBody S10, phase angle will show as zero if: The device was not in research mode Reactance measurement was not activated The parameter was not exported in that testing configuration Software settings suppressed that output 4) Why can't we use phase angle and reactance as a valid measure for checking the data? Reactance alone cannot validate data quality because it is a measure of cell membrane capacity, not an indicator of the device's technical performance. In malnourished children (MAM/SAM), reactance is naturally low due to damaged cell membranes and severe muscle wasting; if you used low reactance as a reason to reject data, you would be accidentally deleting the very children you are trying to study. To validate data, you must look at Resistance and Reactance together (the Impedance Vector) to ensure the electrical signal is consistent, rather than relying on one value that is biologically expected to be abnormal in this population.
